en: Were shattered in the jousting.
Twelve chargers and countless swift horses
Were killed and lay fallen in combat.
Thus my strength proved insufficient.
It seems I have fallen into ruin.
I have none of my former strength;
It seems I am no longer myself.
Our sorrows gathered and overwhelmed us,
And our honor faded away.
You are the strength with which we gird our waists,
Our lioness maiden,
The warrior who brings us blessing.
Grim-featured is Sarybai,
A fearsome enemy such as this.
My charger’s back has grown sore from riding,
And my heart ached from fighting.
My noble steed grew weary,
And my noble head was hard-pressed.
Maiden champion, lioness,
We look to you as our protector.
Should the boastful infidel
Stir up some fresh conflict,
May you deliver the lionhearted warrior
And save him from suffering—
Such is my desire.
For many years before you came,
Against that fiend of surpassing cruelty,
When I thrust willingly, my spear would not pierce;
When I grappled, my strength fell short;
When I struck, my axe would not bite;
When I fired my white musket, its bullet would not pierce.
All the valiant men were destroyed,
And the world cried out that I was dead.
He prolonged the great turmoil,
Dragging maidens away as plunder,
Robbing me of much of my former self,
And thus battering my spirit.
He raided and humiliated us,
And seized my peaceful possessions by force.
When I wrestled him, my strength fell short;
When I struck true, my hand could not penetrate.
Against this infidel Sarybai,
This swaggering warrior,
Khans with sound arms died,
And every soul who grappled with him died.
My surging rage boiled,
But my strength fell short against the hellion;
Thus did my misery boil.”
So spoke Külchoro,
His exhaustion plain to see.
Unable to overcome Sarybai,
Külchoro despaired of life.
As Külchoro stood there,
Speaking softly and casting forth her fortune,
Kuyaly began to speak:
“This is the armor the monster’s infidel son
Wears when he enters combat;
This is the arm with which he wrestles;
That is the man who boasts himself a hero.
I have driven men down and crushed them into disgrace;
I am that wretched warrior.
His origin is alien and his venom strong;
Let us reach that doomed slave
And perish together with him.
I shall settle the proper reckoning;
If he fights, I shall find a way.
If the villain proves obstinate,
We shall gouge out his eyes.
If the villain grows enraged,
We shall lay him out full-length.
Thus shall we take revenge;
If the villain strains against us,
We shall settle his true account.”
She summoned her courage and made ready,
And in place of her former stratagem,
Inspiration came to her from the unseen.
She arranged all her battle gear,
And bloodthirsty Zulpukor
Was fastened bare at her waist.
Without speaking a word,
She growled and worked herself into fury,
Threatening Sarybai.
She thrust out her chest like a hungry lion,
Her eyes wide as an open grave.
The blood drained from her face,
And the sight of her distracted the mind.
If you observed the fierce-eyed maiden,
When she surges against that maiden,
No mortal can stand before her.
Not Sarybai—the whole wide world
Could not confront and defeat her.
With a crest like a fleeing kulan,
A gold-browed, high-arched saddle,
Was fitted upon Zhelzhetpes, swift as the wind,
Like a sovereign ruling a people.
Prancing proudly, Zhelzhetpes
Seemed destined for good fortune.
He champed upon his bit,
And tore the ground wherever he stepped.
The black earth struck by his hooves
Split apart on every side.
His banner-like tail was a piled-up mass,
Revealing the form of a noble steed.
When he strode with bounding steps, the black earth
Scattered like fragments of a great bowl.
A great falcon broad as a house
Shrieked above her head.
She made her charger rear and plunge,
Throwing all the people into an uproar.
“The maiden is a lion!” they said,
Delighting everyone who saw her.
An ancestral spirit descended upon the maiden;
The tasseled banners parted amid the host.
Her majestic presence,
Her bearing upon horseback,
Loomed like a towering mountain.
Every mortal being’s
Wits were utterly confounded.
She looked to either side,
Licking her lips like a hungry lion.
Battle-axe, sword, bow, and arms
Shone all around her.
The enemy who advanced against her
Lost heart and scattered.
Her readiness was plain—
It seemed the fairies themselves escorted her.
And valiant Manas the fierce
Seemed to have become her companion.
Her breast was like a fleeing kulan’s,
Her eyes those of a hunting eagle—
Such was my champion’s aspect.
Over rugged ridges and rocky crags
She had crossed these mountains before.
For many years already,
Against the infidel son of Zhelmoguz,
She had been a seasoned master,
A foe who often fought him.
They were neighbors upon the same land,
Their peoples lived mingled together,
Their herds shared the same pastures,
Their kumis was drunk at common feasts.
They were warriors raised together,
But, growing stubborn, they quarreled,
Struck one another and fought,
And became bitter enemies.
The swaggering champion maiden
Throughout the eighteen thousand worlds
Had stirred up terrible strife.
When she clashed with a giant, she drove him back;
When she grappled with a titan, she overthrew him.
Her name was renowned throughout the world;
The fame of that maiden champion
Had traveled very far.
She was a skillful master of combat,
A champion maiden born but once.
Eight times she had charged.
The maiden attacked Sarybai.
Though she was a woman, the poor soul
Answered him defiantly and hardened herself,
And came to be called the lion maiden.
She was deft and sure with the spear,
Truly knowing all the stratagems of war,
A mighty maiden blessed with fortune.
To the spur where the mountain ended,
To the jutting promontory,
To meet once in eleven years,
At the place where the mountains ended,
They began a campaign and raised a tumult,
Coming there to wage battle.
The accomplished champion Kuyaly
Turned Zhelzhetpes by the reins
And rode out to single combat.
Such was the nature of the conflict.
Sarybai, son of Zhelmoguz,
Was a fiend who had slaughtered many;
At the sight of him, abandon hope of life.
Sarybai, son of Zhelmoguz,
Had grown fierce from drinking blood
And was known among the people as a monster.
When he attacked, he never had his fill of blood;
Once he set upon a man, he never spared his life.
Of all that ears had heard and eyes had seen,
Nothing like him had existed on earth.
Of all the news the people had heard,
Nothing like him had existed among mankind.
His valor was of another kind,
And boundless was his devouring greed.
His charger was swift, and he himself a towering peak;
No such horror existed in the world.
His strength was singular, his venom fierce;
If you saw that infidel before you,
Count yourself dead and abandon hope.
He inflicted tyranny upon the age
And brought humiliation upon mankind.
He began savage conflicts;
Whoever challenged that mad brute,
He slaughtered outright.
He could drink blood and never be sated;
Among all the sons of humankind,
No such creature had ever been born.
Dust rose from those he attacked;
Life fled from those he grappled.
That swine’s ways were unlike all others;
He was born in Zhelpinish,
And the living heard of his wrath.
Does he subdue and seize men—
Was there witchcraft in his mother?
Against that black-hearted swine,
Could anyone who faced him remain alive?
Though a man girded himself, saying, “I am a warrior,”
Could any mortal go against him?
This infidel Sarybai
Was thick-muscled and stone-hearted,
And spread great turmoil through the world.
His cunning was strange, his venom fierce;
When angered and enraged,
He would level the whole wide world.
Upon his two shoulders,
If they rashly ventured there,
Two men apiece could have sat.
At the blaze of his two cheeks,
Six Dhangyt men apiece might feast.
If anyone provoked his anger,
The mortal who grappled with him
He seemed able to swallow, horse and all.
He had a head like half a mountain,
A head like a dog lying down.
He wore a coat broad as ten yurt-roof felts.
His arms were longer than plane trees.
His complexion was strange, his appearance blue-black;
He wore a black iron cap.
His nose was hooked, his face mottled;
His menace was singular, and he was wrath itself.
His nature was corrupt, though he was a warrior;
No mortal dared advance against him.
In Zhelpinish, seventy
Giants had fought him without victory.
A bane to the people, copper-snouted,
No one had seen such a savage face.
No ground remained untrodden by his gray charger;
Nothing on earth remained whole.
Nothing escaped slaughter by the accursed swine;
Nothing among the people remained whole.
When he advanced in a fit of fury,
Even titans scattered without fighting.
From cradles where they lay crying,
Speechless infants were crushed.
Whenever he saw a commotion, he raised his banner;
Against all who challenged him, he raised an uproar.
Titans and giants grieved to face him;
Before that evil, venomous being,
Mortals despaired of life.
Unable to withstand his wrath,
Whole peoples died in combat;
Every person who challenged him died.
No one could endure him.
